findings.claim: In the Eduqas Component 1 Section B exam, you will face two poems you have never seen before. ... The section is worth 20 marks in total. Part (i) asks you to analyse one poem (worth approximately 12 marks), and Part (ii) asks you to compare that poem with a second poem (worth approximately 8 marks).
findings.truth: Unseen poetry is the third section of the second paper, not the second section of the first. The section is worth 40 marks (20% of the GCSE), split 15 marks for the question on the first poem and 25 marks for the second question, which asks for writing about a second poem and a comparison with the first. Every mark figure in the lesson was wrong, and the board is named in student-facing prose.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2: 'Section C (20%) Unseen Poetry (40 marks) ... In the first question, learners will be asked to write about a previously unseen poem. In the second question, learners will be asked to write about a second previously unseen poem, and compare it to the first. ... Section C assesses AO1 and AO2.' Split and timing from the board's own Section C teaching guidance (specimen task): first question [15], comparison question [25], https://www.wjec.co.uk/media/ariif5p5/component-2-section-c-unseen-poetry.pdf

findings.claim: Key Fact: 'Eduqas Component 1 Section B: Part (i) = analyse one poem (~12 marks, AO1 + AO2). Part (ii) = compare with a second poem (~8 marks, AO1 + AO2). No AO3. Total = 20 marks. Spend approximately 15 minutes on Part (i) and 10 minutes on Part (ii).'
findings.truth: Total 40 marks, 15 + 25. The paper itself advises about 20 minutes on the first question and about 40 minutes on the comparison, so the 25-minute allowance taught here is less than half the real one. A student who rehearses this plan writes roughly a third of what the section expects. The AO claim (AO1 and AO2, no AO3) was the only correct part.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Section C as above. Specimen task instruction: 'You are advised to spend about 20 minutes on 31, and about 40 minutes on 32.' (wjec.co.uk Section C guidance PDF, p.6)

findings.claim: What unseen poetry is, how the Eduqas exam works, and a step-by-step approach.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board in student-facing text. Reworded to 'how the exam section works'. Same rule fixed on the lesson 1 flashcard 'How many marks is the Eduqas unseen poetry section?'.

findings.claim: The comparison is worth 8 marks - almost half the section.
findings.truth: The comparison question carries 25 of the 40 marks, so it is more than half the section. 8 out of 20 is also not 'almost half'.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Section C (40 marks); specimen task [15] and [25].

findings.claim: The Eduqas mark scheme rewards: Band 5 - perceptive, detailed analysis ... Band 4 ... Band 3 ... A Band 5 response might say ... A Band 2 response would say ...
findings.truth: Board name plus numbered mark-scheme bands and quoted band wording. Rewritten in the house ladder (top band / upper-mid band / mid band / low band) and in our own words.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT copyright-distancing rule and banned-string list.

findings.claim: 'How many marks is the unseen poetry section worth in total?' - the key marks '20 marks' correct; 40 was not even an option.
findings.truth: 40 marks. Options rebuilt as 20 / 30 / 40 / 50 so that index 2 stays the correct answer.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2: Section C (20%) Unseen Poetry (40 marks).

findings.claim: '20 marks total - Part (i) ~12 marks, Part (ii) ~8 marks.' / 'Approximately 15 minutes.' / 'Approximately 10 minutes.'
findings.truth: 40 marks in total, 15 and 25. About 20 minutes on the first question and about 40 on the comparison.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2; specimen task marks and timing line.

findings.claim: This is what separates Band 5 responses from lower bands.
findings.truth: Numbered band name; replaced with 'top-band responses'.

findings.claim: Q: 'What is the literal meaning of "the city swallowed him whole"?' A: 'He disappeared into the crowd - the city consumed his individuality.'
findings.truth: The second half is a figurative reading, not the literal meaning, in a lesson whose core skill is separating literal meaning from connotation. The lesson body gives the literal meaning as 'the speaker disappears into the city'.
findings.evidence: lesson 2 worked example, narration block n13.

findings.claim: perspective: 'The speaker's attitude towards their subject, conveyed through word choice, imagery, and tone.' (glossary term and the in-text dfn)
findings.truth: That is the definition of tone, not perspective. The lesson's own sentence uses perspective to mean who is speaking and who is addressed, and its practice question says 'perspective (who speaks and to whom)'. Lesson 5's glossary defines it correctly, so lesson 4 was the outlier. A student taught this definition would answer a perspective question by writing about tone.
findings.evidence: lesson 4 narration block n8 and practice question 6; lesson 5 glossary entry 'perspective'.

findings.claim: Part (ii) ... 'This is worth approximately 8 marks and should take about 10 minutes.' Exam tip: 'For 8 marks in 10 minutes, aim for 2 developed paragraphs.' Knowledge check keys '8 marks' correct. Flashcard: '8 marks - about 10 minutes writing time.'
findings.truth: The comparison question is worth 25 marks and the paper advises about 40 minutes on it. The whole lesson scaled the answer to a quarter of its real size, so the two-paragraph framework and the '2-3 points' advice were raised to three or four developed paragraphs. The knowledge check key moved to 25 marks.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Section C (40 marks, two questions, one a comparison); specimen task: comparison question [25], 'about 40 minutes on 32'.

findings.claim: Whole lesson built on 'Timing: Your 25-Minute Plan' and a 3/12/3/7 minute split, repeated in the description, the key facts, the conclusion, three practice questions, two knowledge checks and four flashcards.
findings.truth: The section runs about 60 minutes: about 20 minutes on the first question and about 40 on the comparison. Rebuilt as 4 minutes reading Poem 1, 16 writing the first answer, 5 reading Poem 2, 35 writing the comparison. This was the most mark-costly error in the unit: the lesson trained students to stop writing after a quarter of the available time.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2: Component paper is 2 hours 30 minutes with three equally weighted sections; specimen task timing line 'about 20 minutes on 31, and about 40 minutes on 32'.

findings.claim: Band 5 requires 'perceptive, detailed analysis.' (lesson 6) / 'Band 5 requires depth ...' (lesson 7 conclusion)
findings.truth: Numbered band plus quoted mark-scheme wording. Rewritten in the house ladder and in our own words.

findings.claim: 'Complete a full unseen poetry section in 25 minutes', 'Write a Part (ii) comparison in exactly 7 minutes', 'Annotate this poem in 3 minutes', 'set a 25-minute timer', 'Practise once a week with a 25-minute timer', flashcard '25 minutes.'
findings.truth: A full section is about 60 minutes. Practice timings raised to 60 for the whole section, 35 for the comparison and 4 for annotation, so weekly timed practice matches the real paper.
findings.evidence: specimen task timing line; spec 2.2 section weightings.

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across the seven lessons are labelled '20 marks - Unseen Poetry', two of them '20 marks - Extract Analysis'. Their mark ladders use ranges from the invented split ('Top band (10-12)', 'Top band (7-8)') and close with the banned line 'Band 4-1: Progressively less detailed.'
findings.truth: No question in this section is worth 20 marks and no extract is printed - the poems are the whole text. Labels rebuilt as 15 marks for single-poem questions, 25 marks for comparison questions and 40 marks for the one whole-section task. This label is not cosmetic: js/main.js takes the first number in practice_questions.type to size the AI marking request, so a 25-mark comparison was being marked as a 20-mark answer and a numberless label would fall back to 4 marks. Ladders rebuilt on the real band ranges (13-15 / 10-12 / 7-9 / 4-6 / 1-3 and 21-25 / 16-20 / 11-15 / 6-10 / 1-5) with the house band names.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Section C; specimen task marks and band ranges (wjec.co.uk Section C guidance PDF, pp. 6, 10, 11); js/main.js line 611 marksMatch.

findings.claim: The unit calls the two tasks 'Part (i)' and 'Part (ii)' throughout.
findings.truth: The paper prints them as two separately numbered questions, not parts of one question. The label is a house convention that carries no mark claim, so it is left alone rather than churned through three lessons and their narration. Worth a fleet decision if other unseen-poetry units use different wording.
findings.evidence: specimen task numbers the two tasks 31 and 32.

findings.claim: The checking brief states that the paper is '80 marks across three sections'.
findings.truth: The spec gives three sections of 40 marks each in 2 hours 30 minutes, so 120 marks. No lesson asserts a paper total, so nothing needed editing - flagged only so the brief is corrected for the next unseen-poetry unit.
findings.evidence: spec Summary of Assessment and 2.2: Section A (20%) 40 marks, Section B (20%) 40 marks, Section C (20%) 40 marks; written examination 2 hours 30 minutes, 60% of qualification.

findings.claim: Deliberate departure from the brief's default: the brief said to replace any per-question mark split with a numberless line because the spec does not state one.
findings.truth: The split is verifiable after all. The board's own published Section C teaching guidance prints the specimen task with [15] on the first question and [25] on the comparison, the instruction to spend about 20 and about 40 minutes, and the two band ladders (13-15 down to 1-3, and 21-25 down to 1-5). The lessons therefore assert 15 / 25 and 20 / 40 minutes rather than going numberless. If Tom prefers the numberless line, the figures can be stripped from F1, F2, F7, F11, F12, F14 and F15 without touching anything else.
findings.evidence: https://www.wjec.co.uk/media/ariif5p5/component-2-section-c-unseen-poetry.pdf (WJEC Eduqas GCSE English Literature, Component 2 Section C: Unseen Poetry - examples of questions taken from the specimen assessment materials, pp. 6, 10, 11).

findings.claim: Lesson 7 is titled 'Full Exam Practice' but contains no poems; the practice questions say '[Note: in the actual exam, a poem would be printed here.]'.
findings.truth: Not a factual error, so not edited, but the lesson cannot be completed as written. Two out-of-copyright 20th-century poems, or two public-domain poems with a modern feel, would make it usable. Tom's call.
findings.evidence: lesson 1 practice question 1 and the whole of lesson 7.

summary: Every exam claim in the unit was wrong: the lessons placed unseen poetry in the wrong paper and section, taught a 20-mark section with a 12+8 split (it is 40 marks, 15+25), and built lessons 6 and 7 on a 25-minute plan when the paper allows about 60, so students were trained to write about a third of the expected answer. Lessons 2, 3 and 4 carried no exam-fact errors beyond the unit-wide practice-question labels; their content on language, form and structure checked out. No real poem is quoted anywhere in the unit - every example line is invented - so there was nothing to verify against a source and no copyright exposure.
